Why Can’t I Open My Drawer? Mitigating Object-Driven Shortcuts
in Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition

Geo Ahn Affiliation: Kyung Hee University    Inwoong Lee Affiliation: NAVER Cloud    Taeoh Kim Affiliation: NAVER Cloud    Minho Shim Affiliation: NAVER Cloud    Dongyoon Wee Affiliation: NAVER Cloud    Jinwoo Choi Affiliation: Kyung Hee University
Abstract

We study Compositional Video Understanding (CVU), where models must recognize verbs and objects and compose them to generalize to unseen combinations. We find that existing Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) models fail primarily due to an overlooked failure mode: object-driven verb shortcuts. Through systematic analysis, we show that this behavior arises from two intertwined factors—severe sparsity and skewness of compositional supervision, and the asymmetric learning difficulty between verbs and objects. As training progresses, the existing ZS-CAR model increasingly ignores visual evidence and overfits to co-occurrence statistics. Consequently, the existing model does not gain the benefit of compositional recognition in unseen verb-object compositions. To address this, we propose RCORE, a simple and effective framework that enforces temporally grounded verb learning. RCORE introduces (i) a composition-aware augmentation that diversifies verb–object combinations without corrupting motion cues, and (ii) a temporal order regularization loss that penalizes shortcut behaviors by explicitly modeling temporal structure. Across two benchmarks—Sth-com and our newly constructed EK100-com—RCORE significantly improves unseen composition accuracy, reduces reliance on co-occurrence bias, and achieves consistently positive compositional gaps. Our findings reveal object-driven shortcuts as a critical limiting factor in ZS-CAR and demonstrate that addressing them is essential for robust compositional video understanding. The code is available at https://github.com/KHU-VLL/RCORE.

1 Introduction

Many human actions can be decomposed into two semantic primitives—verbs and objects—and robust video understanding requires recognizing each component and reasoning over their interaction as a composition [12, 22, 7, 8, 2]. Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) formalizes this goal: a model must correctly identify unseen verb–object combinations despite only being exposed to a sparse subset of compositions during training [16].

However, existing ZS-CAR models exhibit a characteristic and persistent failure: they mispredict verbs in unseen compositions by relying on object-driven shortcuts. In other words, rather than learning verb semantics from temporal evidence, models exploit objects as the dominant cue whenever such shortcuts correlate with training labels. To the best of our knowledge, this failure mode has not been explicitly identified or systematically addressed in prior ZS-CAR approaches [16, 14]. We show that this shortcut failure mode arises from two intertwined issues of the ZS-CAR setting: (i) Sparsity and skewness of compositional supervision. The combinatorial nature of verb–object pairs yields extreme under-coverage of the compositional space, e.g. only ∼14.0%\sim 14.0\% label coverage ratio in the Something-Else [22] and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 [7] datasets. This induces strong co-occurrence statistics to the deep learning model as depicted in Figure 1 (a). (ii) Asymmetric learning difficulty between verbs and objects. Objects are recognizable from single frames, while verbs require multi-frame temporal reasoning, as shown in Figure 1 (b). This imbalance naturally encourages models to treat objects as easy predictive shortcuts [25, 17, 32, 11, 30], especially under sparse data regimes.

Our analysis reveals that the existing ZS-CAR model amplifies these issues during training. They increasingly bias predictions toward frequently co-occurring compositions, exhibit growing false-seen and false-co-occurrence prediction ratios, and ultimately yield negative compositional gaps—indicating that they fail to extract any benefit from compositional reasoning beyond independent verb and object recognition. (See Section 3 for details.) These observations call into question the robustness of current ZS-CAR approaches and motivate the need for techniques that explicitly target shortcut mitigation.

We propose RCORE (Robust COmpositional REpresentations), a simple and effective framework designed to mitigate object-driven shortcut and promote temporally grounded verb representations. RCORE consists of two components: (i) a composition-aware augmentation that synthesizes plausible unseen verb–object combinations while preserving the temporal structure of the original video; and (ii) a temporal order regularization objective that penalizes reliance on static cues by contrasting original and perturbed temporal representations. Together, these components address the two root causes of failure in ZS-CAR: compositional sparsity and asymmetric learning difficulty.

Across both datasets, RCORE significantly strengthens verb recognition, reduces co-occurrence bias, produces positive compositional gaps, and improves unseen composition accuracy over strong conditional baselines. Our findings indicate that the primary obstacle in compositional video understanding is not model capacity but model behavior: ZS-CAR models fail because they resort to object-driven shortcuts. By directly tackling this failure mode, RCORE provides a simple path toward more reliable and generalizable ZS-CAR.

In this work, we make the following major contributions:

  • •

    Identifying the core failure mode of ZS-CAR. We show that existing models rely on object-driven verb shortcuts, caused by the sparsity of compositional supervision and the asymmetric learning difficulty between verbs and objects—an issue not explicitly recognized in prior work.

  • •

    Diagnosing limitations of the ZS-CAR evaluation protocol. We reveal that common practices, such as test-set bias calibration, obscure true compositional generalization. To address this, we adopt an open-world unbiased evaluation setting and introduce the compositional gap metric to measure the benefit of compositional reasoning.

  • •

    A simple yet effective framework that mitigates shortcut learning. We propose RCORE, which comprises a composition-aware augmentation and a temporal order regularization loss (TORC) to promote temporally grounded verb representations under compositional sparsity. Through experiments on Sth-com and our new EK100-com dataset, we demonstrate that RCORE shows consistently favorable performance improvements across diverse evaluation scenarios, metrics, and datasets.

2 Related Work

Zero-shot compositional action recognition. Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) [16] aims to generalize to novel verb–object combinations not seen during training. Unlike zero-shot (or open-set) action recognition [5, 4, 40], ZS-CAR retains the same verb and object classes across train and test splits and evaluates a model’s ability to compose known primitives. It addresses the performance degradation issue on novel unseen combinations of known concepts, which arises from the model’s lack of compositional generalization ability. Conditional learning [16, 13] has been effective for estimating joint verb–object probabilities, while other work [14] pursues improved feature disentanglement. However, as our analysis reveals in Section 3 and Section 5.2, these approaches remain susceptible to object-driven shortcut behavior and progressively overfit co-occurrence statistics.

Compositional zero-shot Learning in image understanding.

Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) has been widely studied in the image domain [23, 24, 21, 34, 36, 26]. CZSL enables models to recognize novel combinations of previously learned primitive concepts, such as objects and their states. Prior works have approached this problem through feature disentanglement [29, 42], modular architectures [27], and CLIP-based prompt learning [26, 18]. Unlike image-based CZSL, ZS-CAR requires modeling temporal dynamics for verbs, making the problem fundamentally different. Our work focuses specifically on the video domain and highlights a failure mode—object-driven verb shortcuts—that does not arise in image-only CZSL.

Shortcut learning.

Shortcut learning is a pervasive issue in visual recognition. Several studies show that models tend to rely on easy-example biases [35, 15, 30] or easier-to-learn cues—such as color or texture—when these cues correlate with labels [25, 11]. A line of work attributes this behavior to co-occurrence statistics in the training data [1, 32]. In video understanding, similar shortcut behaviors occur when action models rely on backgrounds rather than motion [17, 6, 33, 9, 2]. Building on these observations, we argue that ZS-CAR introduces an additional structural imbalance: verbs require temporal reasoning, whereas objects can be recognized from a single frame. This learning asymmetry amplifies shortcut tendencies and leads models to predict verbs primarily from object cues—a failure mode we diagnose and directly address in this work.

3 Diagnosis: Why ZS-CAR Models Fail?

3.1 Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition

We study Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) [16], where the goal is to recognize verb–object compositions that might never appear in the training set. Let 𝕐V\mathbb{Y}^{V} and 𝕐O\mathbb{Y}^{O} denote the sets of verb and object labels, and let each action label be a pair 𝐲=(𝐲V,𝐲O)∈𝕐V×𝕐O\mathbf{y}=(\mathbf{y}^{V},\mathbf{y}^{O})\in\mathbb{Y}^{V}\times\mathbb{Y}^{O}. The training set is 𝔻train={(𝐗i,𝐲i)}i=1N\mathbb{D}_{\text{train}}=\{(\mathbf{X}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, and its set of observed (seen) compositions is 𝕐seen={𝐲i∣(𝐗i,𝐲i)∈𝔻train}\mathbb{Y}_{\text{seen}}=\{\mathbf{y}_{i}\mid(\mathbf{X}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})\in\mathbb{D}_{\text{train}}\}. We define the validation and test sets analogously. The validation and test sets contain both seen and unseen compositions, enabling evaluation of compositional generalization. ZS-CAR therefore measures whether a model can correctly compose familiar verbs and objects into novel pairs at test time.

3.2 Diagnostic Metrics

For better understanding the underlying behavior of ZS-CAR models, we present two diagnostic metrics: (1) training bias metrics to measure a model’s overfitting and (2) Compositional Gap to assess the benefits of compositional modeling.

Training bias metrics

To measure how the model overfits to the training set statistics, we introduce two types of misclassification ratios: False Seen Prediction and False Co-occurrence Prediction ratios. False Seen Prediction (FSP) ratio denotes the ratio of unseen composition samples incorrectly predicted to seen composition labels. Out of these mispredicted samples, False Co-occurrence Prediction (FCP) ratio is likewise defined as the proportion of those assigned to frequently co-occurring labels. Here, a composition label is considered ‘frequently co-occurring’ if its occurrence is higher than one standard deviation above the mean frequency in the training data.

Compositional Gap

We introduce Compositional Gap to examine whether a model genuinely benefits from understanding videos in a compositional manner. Compositional Gap (ΔCG\Delta_{\text{CG}}) is defined as

ΔCG=AccC−(AccV×AccO),\Delta_{\text{CG}}=\mathrm{Acc}^{C}-(\mathrm{Acc}^{V}\times\mathrm{Acc}^{O}), (1)

where AccC\text{Acc}^{C} is the composition accuracy (%) computed from the logits over the composition space, whereas AccV\text{Acc}^{V} and AccO\text{Acc}^{O} are the verb and object accuracies (%) derived from the logits over their individual component spaces. A positive ΔCG\Delta_{\text{CG}} indicates that the model truly gains an advantage from its compositional architecture.

3.3 Empirical Diagnosis of Object-driven Shortcuts in ZS-CAR

In this section, we systematically diagnose the key failure mode in ZS-CAR—object-driven shortcuts. We demonstrate that these shortcuts prevent ZS-CAR models from learning robust verb representations, consequently leading to poor generalization to unseen compositions. We present additional evidence of object-driven shortcut learning in ZS-CAR models in Section 5 and the supplementary material.

Objects are easier to learn than verbs.

To investigate the learning difficulty of verbs and objects, we train a randomly initialized model on a subset of Sth-com [16]. Based on the observation that the easier-to-learn cue is captured earlier and exhibits higher accuracy [25], we can analyze the learning difficulty of each component. In Figure 2 (a), the results show a clear trend: the model learns objects faster and consistently achieves higher accuracy for objects than for verbs. While intuitively expected, these results empirically verify that objects are inherently easier to learn than verbs in compositional action recognition.

Object-driven shortcuts in ZS-CAR

Under strong co-occurrence priors, models choose shortcuts emerged from easier-to-learn cues, rather than learn robust representations [25, 30, 11, 3, 17, 6]. We argue this shortcut learning behavior accelerates in ZS-CAR due to the asymmetric learning difficulty. To verify this, inspired by prior work [30], we train models on a perfectly biased training set and test on two distinct splits—bias-aligned seen compositions and bias-conflict unseen compositions— utilizing Sth-com [16]. As shown in Figure 2 (b), in the both cases of the randomly initialized ViT [10] and CLIP [28], the object accuracies for unseen compositions increased as the seen composition accuracies also increased, while the verb accuracies for unseen compositions drop under the random accuracy. Paradoxically, CLIP [16], well-known for its superior representational power, exhibits the highest object accuracy (94.0%) and the lowest verb accuracy (1.9%) concurrently on unseen compositions. These results demonstrate models tend to fall into object-driven shortcuts to exploit co-occurrence priors in the training data, resulting in poor verb representations.

Object-driven shortcuts directly harm unseen generalization.

Next, we investigate whether the state-of-the-art (SOTA) model also fails to generalize to unseen compositions as a consequence of these object-driven shortcuts. As shown in Figure 3, we trace the validation accuracies along with FSP and FCP ratios—metrics designed to quantify the model’s reliance on the training statistics—of C2C [16] throughout the training progress on Sth-com [16]. The clear correlation between increased FSP/FCP ratios and widen seen-unseen accuracy gap indicates that the model overfits to the training statistics.

Compositional Gap reveals the SOTA model fails to benefit from compositional modeling.

We evaluate the Compositional Gap (ΔCG\Delta_{\text{CG}}) performance of current SOTA ZS-CAR model [16]. As shown in Table 1, the model shows a negative ΔCG\Delta_{\text{CG}} on unseen compositions in Sth-com [16]. This demonstrates that, without addressing these shortcuts, the SOTA model gains no advantage from compositional modeling compared to independent modeling for unseen compositions.

4 RCORE

We introduce RCORE, a learning framework that mitigates object-driven shortcut learning in zero-shot compositional action recognition. RCORE improves compositional generalization by strengthening verb–object representations under sparse supervision through two complementary components: (i) VOCAMix, a composition-aware augmentation that expands the variety of verb–object combinations, and (ii) TORC, a temporal order regularization loss that promotes temporally grounded verb learning over static object cues. Following prior work [16], we use AIM [37], a CLIP-based [28] parameter-efficient spatio-temporal encoder, as our backbone. Figure 4 (a) gives an overview of RCORE.

4.2 Temporal Order Regularization Loss

TORC loss forces the model to rely on temporal structure: it penalizes alignment with temporally incorrect feature sequences and suppresses confident verb predictions when temporal ordering is corrupted. This regularization steers the model away from static object cues and strengthens temporally grounded verb representations.

5 Experimental Results

In this section, we conduct rigorous experiments to address the following research questions: (1) Do conventional ZS-CAR evaluation protocols faithfully reveal true model behavior? If not, what is a more appropriate protocol for exposing real generalization performance? (Section 5.1) (2) Does the proposed compositional gap (CG) metric reveal whether a model actually benefits from compositional understanding beyond independent verb/object predictions? (Section 5.2 and Section 5.3) (3) Does RCORE mitigate the two key failure modes—co-occurrence overfitting and object-driven verb shortcuts—identified in our diagnosis? (Section 5.2) (4) Do these improvements translate to consistent gains across datasets? (Section 5.3) (5) How does each proposed component contribute to robust compositional learning? (Section 5.4) We describe the experimental setup and then report results aligned with these questions.

5.1 Experimental setup

Limitations of conventional ZS-CAR evaluation.

Existing ZS-CAR works [16, 13, 14] rely on the closed-world protocol, where inference is restricted to a small set of compositions that appear in the validation or test split. This protocol hides a model’s incorrect tendency to over-predict seen compositions and obscures co-occurrence-driven behaviors. A more serious methodological flaw is the use of test-set–tuned bias calibration. Selecting the bias term with access to test labels systematically inflates unseen accuracy and prevents meaningful comparison across methods.

Our evaluation setup.

To expose genuine generalization, we adopt an open-world, unbiased protocol by default: (i) inference spans the full space 𝕐V×𝕐O\mathbb{Y}^{V}\times\mathbb{Y}^{O}, and (ii) no test labels are used to tune biases. We also report: (a) open-world biased results using a realistic validation set-tuned bias, and (b) closed-world H.M. and AUC for comparison with existing methods. All results in Section 3 also follow the default open-world, unbiased protocol.

Datasets. We evaluate on two ZS-CAR benchmarks: Sth-com [16] and our curated EK100-com. Sth-com is derived from Something-Something V2 [12] and Something-Else [22], containing 79K videos with 161 verbs and 248 objects. Following prior work [39, 31], we also evaluate on the Temporal subset consisting of verbs requiring temporal reasoning. We additionally introduce the EPIC-KITCHENS-100-composition (EK100-com) benchmark, constructed by repurposing EPIC-KITCHENS-100 [7] following the Sth-com protocol. EK100-com includes 71K egocentric videos, 82 verbs, and 228 objects. Full construction details are provided in the Section A.

Evaluation metrics.

We report top-1 composition, verb, and object accuracy on seen and unseen compositions, along with their harmonic mean (H.M.). We also measure the compositional gap ΔCG\Delta_{\mathrm{CG}} (1) which indicates whether a model benefits from compositional reasoning beyond independent verb/object predictions. (see Section 3) A higher ΔCG\Delta_{\mathrm{CG}} reflects stronger compositional synergy.

Baselines.

We primarily compare RCORE against C2C [16], the current SOTA ZS-CAR method. To isolate the effect of conditional learning, we also evaluate two independent baselines. AIM [37] is the CLIP [28]-based spatio-temporal adapter model used as our backbone. C2C w/o conditioning augments AIM with all architectural components of C2C except the conditional modeling itself. We additionally include closed-world results of a recent ZS-CAR approach [14].

5.2 Analysis

In this section, we validate that our RCORE framework effectively addresses the two key challenges in ZS-CAR—(i) reliance on co-occurrence statistics and (ii) object-driven shortcuts in verb learning—and achieves improved compositional representations compared to the baseline [16].

Overcoming reliance on co-occurrence statistics.

In Figure 5 (a), we present the False Co-occurrence Prediction (FCP) curves of RCORE and the baseline [16] on Sth-com. While the baseline’s FCP ratio increases substantially during training (11% →\rightarrow 17%), the FCP of RCORE decreases (9% →\rightarrow 8%), indicating that RCORE is markedly less dependent on co-occurrence statistics.

Addressing object-driven shortcuts.

In Figure 5 (b), we compare the cosine similarity between the original verb features 𝐟V\mathbf{f}^{V} and the reversed verb features 𝐟revV\mathbf{f}^{V}_{\text{rev}} for RCORE and the baseline [16] over the course of training. While the baseline [16] maintains a high cosine similarity (0.910.91) due to its reliance on object-driven shortcuts, RCORE drives this value to a strongly negative (−0.73-0.73), successfully distinguishing opposite temporal semantics such as ’opening’ vs.’closing’.

In Figure 6, we further visualize this behavior through verb confusion matrices on the Sth-com [16] test set. RCORE cleanly separates pairs of opposite verbs, while C2C [16] frequently confuses them, e.g. misclassifying ‘unfolding’ as ‘folding’. These results collectively demonstrate that C2C fails to overcome the critical challenge of object-driven shortcuts in verb learning, whereas RCORE directly targets this failure mode and learns verb representations that generalize robustly to unseen compositions.

The learned verb representations are indeed effective.

We further assess the quality of the learned verb representations by evaluating temporal modeling ability on the Temporal subset of Sth-com [16], as shown in Figure 5 (c). Across both seen and unseen compositions, RCORE exhibits a substantially larger performance gap between original and shuffled features. Improved unseen generalization.

In Figure 5 (a), we present the learning curve of our RCORE and the baseline [16] on Sth-com. Addressing the two key challenges in ZS-CAR, RCORE significantly improves unseen composition accuracy upon the baseline. While the baseline significantly increases FCP ratio from 10.8% at 5 epochs to 16.8% at 25 epochs, we observe our RCORE reports FCP ratio values of 10.8% at 5 epochs and 8.7% at 25 epochs, demonstrating stable mitigation of the co-occurrence bias. 5.4 Ablation Studies

Effects of RCORE components.

In Table 4 (a), we investigate the effect of each component in our RCORE framework. When used individually, TORC loss is the most effective by providing explicit temporal modeling objectives. Notably, it significantly improves verb recognition performances across both seen and unseen compositions (63.6% vs. 65.7% on seen compositions and 54.4% vs. 56.8% on unseen compositions). Importantly, we can achieve the highest ZS-CAR performance by employing all three components together during training. This synergistic improvement is achieved by effectively tackling dataset sparsity with VOCAMix, reinforcing temporal order modeling with TORC, and alleviating co-occurrence bias with Margin loss.

Effects of TORC components.

Table 4 (b) evaluates the roles of LcosL_{\cos}, which enforces discrimination of opposite temporal semantics, and LentL_{\text{ent}}, which prevents reliance on static cues. We show the each component of TORC can encourage performance improvement. Each term individually improves performance, while using both together yields the largest gains in unseen verb accuracy.

Effects of VOCAMix.

In Table 4 (c), we validate the effectiveness of our proposed composition-aware VOCAMix by comparing it with widely adopted mixing augmentations. We argue that conventional image-based augmentations are insufficient for composition verb-object learning. Specifically, CutMix [38] allows for mixing backgrounds with corresponding labels and Mixup [41] blends verbs and objects concurrently, failing to preserve the temporal difference information that is essential for verb recognition. As a result, these methods yield a lower H.M. score than the baseline. In contrast, our VOCAMix, aiming to generate realistic unseen composition samples, shows modest performance gains over the baseline. Furthermore, we observe that mixing a static frame into the estimated foreground region shows additional performance boost (+0.2 points in the H.M.) over applying it to the entire background (denoted as ‘VOCAMix w/o F.E.’).

Effects of Margin loss.

In Table 4 (d), we validate the effectiveness of our proposed Margin loss. To mitigate the model’s reliance on dataset co-occurrence priors while maintaining baseline performance, we employ our method and validate its effectiveness by comparing it with the widely-used large-margin softmax loss. The large-margin softmax (L-softmax) [19] loss is implemented by multiplying the angle θ\theta between the input feature vector and the target classifier by a margin mm (e.g., cos⁡(m​θ)\cos(m\theta)), thereby forcing the model to learn stricter decision boundaries with narrower angular margins. We apply this L-softmax loss into composition classification loss, consistent with the implementation schedule of our Margin loss. Compared to the L-softmax [19] approach, our proposed Margin loss successfully reduces FCP ratio while preserving performance. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our strategy, which selectively targets frequent-but-incorrect logits not the entire logits.

6 Conclusions

We revisit zero-shot compositional action recognition and show that existing methods fail mainly due to object-driven shortcuts, stemming from compositional sparsity and the asymmetric difficulty of learning verbs versus objects. We also find that the widely used closed-world, test-tuned evaluation protocol conceals this failure, overstating model generalization. We introduce RCORE, a simple framework that targets these issues directly: VOCAMix enlarges the effective compositional support, and TORC loss enforces temporal order sensitivity to reduce reliance on static object cues. Across two benchmarks and under a realistic open-world, unbiased evaluation setting, RCORE consistently improves unseen composition recognition performances, indicating genuine compositional reasoning. Our results highlight that both proper evaluation and shortcut-aware training are essential for progress in compositional video understanding.

Appendix A Details on EK100-com dataset

In this section, we provide details about our curated ZS-CAR benchmark, EPIC-KITCHENS-100-composition (EK100-com). We construct EK100-com by repurposing EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (EK100) [7] following the same protocol of constructing Sth-com [16]. In particular, we use the original training (67217 samples) and validation (9668 samples) split of EK100 [7] and split them as follows: (1) we filter the data to include only compositions with more than five samples each. (2) we ensure that all compositions present in the validation set also exist in the training set. After initial filtering, the training set comprises 62,790 samples with 1,331 unique compositions and the validation set contains 8,657 samples, which consist of 833 seen compositions and 3 unseen compositions. (3) we randomly select half of the compositions from both the training and validation sets and swap these subsets. (4) Finally, we split the validation and test set with a ratio of 3:43:4. We provide the statistics of EK100-com in Table 5 and Figure 7, and some seen/unseen composition examples of EK100-com in Figure 8.

Beyond expanding the pool of publicly available ZS-CAR benchmarks, our repurposed EK100-com exhibits two key properties that make it a compelling ZS-CAR benchmark. First, unlike Something-Something V2 [12], where videos may involve multiple objects associated with a verb, videos in EK100 [7] depict actions consisting of a single verb and a single object. Therefore, the training data of EK100-com provides explicit object supervision for the models. Second, since EK100 [7] has long-tailed distribution, the label coverage ratio of EK100-com is 7.5%, which is much lower than that of Sth-com [16] (12.8%). This makes EK100-com a challenging benchmark, suitable for evaluating whether a model can overcome the risk of shortcut learning induced by data sparsity.

B.2 Implementation details on RCORE

Experimental Setup.

We implement our method using PyTorch and conduct all experiments on 8 NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs. For video preprocessing, we uniformly sample frames from each video to generate clips of size 3×16×224×2243\times 16\times 224\times 224 (channels ×\times frames ×\times height ×\times width).

Model Architecture.

We utilize CLIP-B/16 [28] as our visual/text backbone. Following prior work [16], we adopt AIM [37], a parameter-efficient spatio-temporal adapter for CLIP [28], as the video encoder. We also construct the verb encoder with two temporal convolution layers with ReLU activations, while the object encoder employs temporal average pooling followed by a two-layer MLP with ReLU activations. We use CoOp-style [43] learnable text prompts for all models.

Training Strategy.

We train all models, including baselines and RCORE, for 30 epochs with a total batch size of 128. The base learning rate is set to 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} for Sth-com [16] and 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} for EK100-com, initialized with a 3-epoch warmup. Following prior work [16], we adopt closed-world training setting. We empirically find that setting the softmax temperature to 0.07, same as the implementation of CLIP [28], results in better ZS-CAR performance than the value of 0.01, used in prior work [16]. Therefore, we adopt this temperature value for both C2C [16] and RCORE, except for the case of AIM [37] with independent modeling. For VOCAMix, we employ the unsupervised foreground estimation algorithm FAME [9] to identify high-motion regions. FAME [9] isolates the moving foreground from background regions based on frame differences and color statistics. To generate the mixed samples, we first sample the mixing coefficient from a Beta​(2.0,2.0)\text{Beta}(2.0,2.0) distribution, following prior work [38, 41]. We then scale it by 0.2 for Sth-com [16] and 0.5 for EK100-com to obtain the final blending coefficient λ\lambda. We summarize the hyperparameters used in this work in Table 6.

Loss configuration.

For the total loss, we set the weights for the verb and object components to α=0.2\alpha=0.2 and for the composition loss to β=1.0\beta=1.0, following prior work [16]. As demonstrated in Table 9 (g) and (h), we empirically find it beneficial to linearly warm up the weights for the auxiliary losses: γ\gamma is increased from 0.0 to 1.0 over 5 epoch to 10 epoch, and δ\delta from 0.0 to 0.8 over epochs 15 epoch to 20 epoch.

Inference.

During inference, we adopt a single-view, single-crop protocol. For bias calibration, we select the bias term that maximizes the harmonic mean of the accuracies for seen and unseen compositions.

Appendix C Additional Evidence of Object-Driven Shortcuts

In this section, we provide further evidence demonstrating that existing ZS-CAR learning approaches are susceptible to object-driven shortcut learning.

Failure case analysis of the existing ZS-CAR model.

In Table 7 and Table 8, we investigate top-10 failure cases of the model trained with the existing ZS-CAR learning approach [16]. The top-10 failure cases shown in the Table 7 constitute 9.5% of the misclassifications on unseen compositions for Sth-com [16], compared to 49% for EK100-com as shown in Table 8. For the analysis of Sth-com [16], we exclude ambiguous cases arising from annotation issues to obtain meaningful results. A prime example is the top-1 failure case, (‘Covering [something] with [something]’, ‘Paper’), where 66% of the errors are misclassified as ‘Pencil’. Upon visual inspection, we confirm that nearly all these videos actually depict the action of covering a pencil with paper. In Table 7 and Table 8, we observe a common tendency across both datasets: the model frequently misclassifies verbs as their temporally reversed or opposing counterparts. Specifically, we demonstrate that these mispredictions stem from the model’s reliance on co-occurrence statistics. For instance, the model misclassifies unseen ‘(Closing, Drawer)’ samples as ‘(Opening, Drawer)’, which accounts for 36% of the errors. Notably, ‘Opening’ is the verb most frequently paired with ‘Drawer’ in the training set. These findings suggest that the model has failed to learn robust verb representations that generalize to unseen compositions, largely due to object-driven shortcut learning.

We compare the baseline’s temporal average pooling with attention pooling (Attn. pool). In attention pooling, a linear layer computes frame-wise attention weights from the input verb feature sequences, aggregating them via a weighted sum to obtain the final verb feature for classification. While attention pooling yields a slight improvement in verb accuracy, it fails to reduce the compositional gap (ΔC​G\Delta_{CG}) on unseen compositions. In contrast, our TORC loss achieves significant improvements in H.M. with both aggregation methods. Notably, the combination of temporal average pooling and TORC loss enables the model to overcome the negative compositional gap.

In Table 9 (e), we investigate the impact of the hyperparameter KK, which determines the number of top-ranked logits to which the Margin loss is applied. We find that applying the margin selectively to the frequent-but-incorrect logits within the top-10 (K=10K=10) reports the highest H.M., outperforming the approach of applying it to all seen composition logits (K=3451K=3451) (36.4% vs. 35.5%). This suggests that penalizing only the most confusing candidates—specifically those that frequently co-occur with the input components—effectively mitigates co-occurrence bias without compromising the model’s overall performance. For instance, given an input like ‘(Pretending to tear, Paper)’, our intention is to penalize plausible but incorrect distractors such as ‘(Tearing, Paper)’ or ‘(Folding, Paper)’, while avoiding penalties on irrelevant classes like ‘(Throwing, Paper)’ that are already ranked low.

In Table 9 (g), we observe that introducing the explicit temporal order modeling task via TORC starting from 5 epoch, after initial training, is effective. In particular, the strategy of linearly increasing the loss weight from epoch 5 to 10 is the most effective, resulting in 1.7 point boost in H.M. compared to the baseline. Finally, in Table 9 (h), we analyze the impact of scaling the weight of our Margin loss, revealing a trade-off between improved unseen composition accuracy and decreased seen composition accuracy. We observe that applying Margin loss starting from epoch 15, the point at which the model begins to overfit the training data as shown in Figure 3 of the main paper, is more effective than starting from the earlier epoch. We also find that linearly scaling the loss weight over 5 epochs is the most effective strategy to maintain the model’s performance.

We present extended results corresponding to the experiment shown in Figure 5 (c) of the main paper, including all versions of the Temporal/Static split. Sevilla et al. [31] originally defined these splits based on cognitive science experiments on Something-Something V2 [12] verb classes: a Temporal split (18 verbs) where temporal information matters, and a Static split (18 verbs) where such information is redundant. Abstract
We study Compositional Video Understanding (CVU), where models must recognize verbs and objects and compose them to generalize to unseen combinations.
We find that existing Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) models fail primarily due to an overlooked failure mode: object-driven verb shortcuts .
Through systematic analysis, we show that this behavior arises from two intertwined factors—severe sparsity and skewness of compositional supervision, and the asymmetric learning difficulty between verbs and objects.
As training progresses, the existing ZS-CAR model increasingly ignores visual evidence and overfits to co-occurrence statistics.
Consequently, the existing model does not gain the benefit of compositional recognition in unseen verb-object compositions.
To address this, we propose RCORE , a simple and effective framework that enforces temporally grounded verb learning.
RCORE introduces (i) a composition-aware augmentation that diversifies verb–object combinations without corrupting motion cues, and (ii) a temporal order regularization loss that penalizes shortcut behaviors by explicitly modeling temporal structure.
Across two benchmarks—Sth-com and our newly constructed EK100-com— RCORE significantly improves unseen composition accuracy, reduces reliance on co-occurrence bias, and achieves consistently positive compositional gaps.
Our findings reveal object-driven shortcuts as a critical limiting factor in ZS-CAR and demonstrate that addressing them is essential for robust compositional video understanding.
The code is available at https://github.com/KHU-VLL/RCORE .

1 Introduction
Many human actions can be decomposed into two semantic primitives—verbs and objects—and robust video understanding requires recognizing each component and reasoning over their interaction as a composition [ 12 , 22 , 7 , 8 , 2 ] .
Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) formalizes this goal: a model must correctly identify unseen verb–object combinations despite only being exposed to a sparse subset of compositions during training [ 16 ] .
However, existing ZS-CAR models exhibit a characteristic and persistent failure: they mispredict verbs in unseen compositions by relying on object-driven shortcuts .
In other words, rather than learning verb semantics from temporal evidence, models exploit objects as the dominant cue whenever such shortcuts correlate with training labels.
To the best of our knowledge, this failure mode has not been explicitly identified or systematically addressed in prior ZS-CAR approaches [ 16 , 14 ] .
We show that this shortcut failure mode arises from two intertwined issues of the ZS-CAR setting:
(i) Sparsity and skewness of compositional supervision.
The combinatorial nature of verb–object pairs yields extreme under-coverage of the compositional space, e.g . only ∼ 14.0 % \sim 14.0\% label coverage ratio in the Something-Else [ 22 ] and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 [ 7 ] datasets.
This induces strong co-occurrence statistics to the deep learning model as depicted in Figure 1 (a).
(ii) Asymmetric learning difficulty between verbs and objects.
Objects are recognizable from single frames, while verbs require multi-frame temporal reasoning, as shown in Figure 1 (b).
This imbalance naturally encourages models to treat objects as easy predictive shortcuts [ 25 , 17 , 32 , 11 , 30 ] , especially under sparse data regimes.
Our analysis reveals that the existing ZS-CAR model amplifies these issues during training.
They increasingly bias predictions toward frequently co-occurring compositions, exhibit growing false-seen and false-co-occurrence prediction ratios, and ultimately yield negative compositional gaps —indicating that they fail to extract any benefit from compositional reasoning beyond independent verb and object recognition. (See Section 3 for details.)
These observations call into question the robustness of current ZS-CAR approaches and motivate the need for techniques that explicitly target shortcut mitigation.
We propose RCORE (Robust COmpositional REpresentations), a simple and effective framework designed to mitigate object-driven shortcut and promote temporally grounded verb representations.
RCORE consists of two components:
(i) a composition-aware augmentation that synthesizes plausible unseen verb–object combinations while preserving the temporal structure of the original video; and
(ii) a temporal order regularization objective that penalizes reliance on static cues by contrasting original and perturbed temporal representations.
Together, these components address the two root causes of failure in ZS-CAR: compositional sparsity and asymmetric learning difficulty.
Across both datasets, RCORE significantly strengthens verb recognition, reduces co-occurrence bias, produces positive compositional gaps, and improves unseen composition accuracy over strong conditional baselines.
Our findings indicate that the primary obstacle in compositional video understanding is not model capacity but model behavior: ZS-CAR models fail because they resort to object-driven shortcuts.
By directly tackling this failure mode, RCORE provides a simple path toward more reliable and generalizable ZS-CAR.

In this work, we make the following major contributions:
•
Identifying the core failure mode of ZS-CAR.
We show that existing models rely on object-driven verb shortcuts , caused by the sparsity of compositional supervision and the asymmetric learning difficulty between verbs and objects—an issue not explicitly recognized in prior work.
•
Diagnosing limitations of the ZS-CAR evaluation protocol.
We reveal that common practices, such as test-set bias calibration, obscure true compositional generalization.
To address this, we adopt an open-world unbiased evaluation setting and introduce the compositional gap metric to measure the benefit of compositional reasoning.
•
A simple yet effective framework that mitigates shortcut learning.
We propose RCORE , which comprises a composition-aware augmentation and a temporal order regularization loss (TORC) to promote temporally grounded verb representations under compositional sparsity.
Through experiments on Sth-com and our new EK100-com dataset, we demonstrate that RCORE shows consistently favorable performance improvements across diverse evaluation scenarios, metrics, and datasets.
2 Related Work
Zero-shot compositional action recognition.
Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) [ 16 ] aims to generalize to novel verb–object combinations not seen during training.
Unlike zero-shot (or open-set) action recognition [ 5 , 4 , 40 ] , ZS-CAR retains the same verb and object classes across train and test splits and evaluates a model’s ability to compose known primitives.
It addresses the performance degradation issue on novel unseen combinations of known concepts, which arises from the model’s lack of compositional generalization ability.
Conditional learning [ 16 , 13 ] has been effective for estimating joint verb–object probabilities, while other work [ 14 ] pursues improved feature disentanglement.
However, as our analysis reveals in Section 3 and Section 5.2 , these approaches remain susceptible to object-driven shortcut behavior and progressively overfit co-occurrence statistics.
Compositional zero-shot Learning in image understanding.
Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) has been widely studied in the image domain [ 23 , 24 , 21 , 34 , 36 , 26 ] .
CZSL enables models to recognize novel combinations of previously learned primitive concepts, such as objects and their states.
Prior works have approached this problem through feature disentanglement [ 29 , 42 ] , modular architectures [ 27 ] , and CLIP-based prompt learning [ 26 , 18 ] .
Unlike image-based CZSL, ZS-CAR requires modeling temporal dynamics for verbs, making the problem fundamentally different.
Our work focuses specifically on the video domain and highlights a failure mode—object-driven verb shortcuts—that does not arise in image-only CZSL.
Shortcut learning.
Shortcut learning is a pervasive issue in visual recognition.
Several studies show that models tend to rely on easy-example biases [ 35 , 15 , 30 ] or easier-to-learn cues—such as color or texture—when these cues correlate with labels [ 25 , 11 ] .
A line of work attributes this behavior to co-occurrence statistics in the training data [ 1 , 32 ] .
In video understanding, similar shortcut behaviors occur when action models rely on backgrounds rather than motion [ 17 , 6 , 33 , 9 , 2 ] .
Building on these observations, we argue that ZS-CAR introduces an additional structural imbalance: verbs require temporal reasoning, whereas objects can be recognized from a single frame.
This learning asymmetry amplifies shortcut tendencies and leads models to predict verbs primarily from object cues—a failure mode we diagnose and directly address in this work.
3 Diagnosis: Why ZS-CAR Models Fail?
3.1 Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition

3.2 Diagnostic Metrics
For better understanding the underlying behavior of ZS-CAR models, we present two diagnostic metrics: (1) training bias metrics to measure a model’s overfitting and (2) Compositional Gap to assess the benefits of compositional modeling.
Training bias metrics
To measure how the model overfits to the training set statistics, we introduce two types of misclassification ratios: False Seen Prediction and False Co-occurrence Prediction ratios.
False Seen Prediction (FSP) ratio denotes the ratio of unseen composition samples incorrectly predicted to seen composition labels.
Out of these mispredicted samples, False Co-occurrence Prediction (FCP) ratio is likewise defined as the proportion of those assigned to frequently co-occurring labels.
Here, a composition label is considered ‘frequently co-occurring’ if its occurrence is higher than one standard deviation above the mean frequency in the training data.

3.3 Empirical Diagnosis of Object-driven Shortcuts in ZS-CAR
In this section, we systematically diagnose the key failure mode in ZS-CAR—object-driven shortcuts.
We demonstrate that these shortcuts prevent ZS-CAR models from learning robust verb representations, consequently leading to poor generalization to unseen compositions.
We present additional evidence of object-driven shortcut learning in ZS-CAR models in Section 5 and the supplementary material.
Objects are easier to learn than verbs.
To investigate the learning difficulty of verbs and objects, we train a randomly initialized model on a subset of Sth-com [ 16 ] .
Based on the observation that the easier-to-learn cue is captured earlier and exhibits higher accuracy [ 25 ] , we can analyze the learning difficulty of each component.
In Figure 2 (a), the results show a clear trend: the model learns objects faster and consistently achieves higher accuracy for objects than for verbs.
While intuitively expected, these results empirically verify that objects are inherently easier to learn than verbs in compositional action recognition.
Object-driven shortcuts in ZS-CAR
Under strong co-occurrence priors, models
choose shortcuts emerged from easier-to-learn cues, rather than learn robust representations [ 25 , 30 , 11 , 3 , 17 , 6 ] .
We argue this shortcut learning behavior accelerates in ZS-CAR due to the asymmetric learning difficulty.
To verify this, inspired by prior work [ 30 ] , we train models on a perfectly biased training set and test on two distinct splits—bias-aligned seen compositions and bias-conflict unseen compositions— utilizing Sth-com [ 16 ] .
As shown in Figure 2 (b), in the both cases of the randomly initialized ViT [ 10 ] and CLIP [ 28 ] , the object accuracies for unseen compositions increased as the seen composition accuracies also increased, while the verb accuracies for unseen compositions drop under the random accuracy.
Paradoxically, CLIP [ 16 ] , well-known for its superior representational power, exhibits the highest object accuracy (94.0%) and the lowest verb accuracy (1.9%) concurrently on unseen compositions.
These results demonstrate models tend to fall into object-driven shortcuts to exploit co-occurrence priors in the training data, resulting in poor verb representations.

4 RCORE
We introduce RCORE , a learning framework that mitigates object-driven shortcut learning in zero-shot compositional action recognition.
RCORE improves compositional generalization by strengthening verb–object representations under sparse supervision through two complementary components:
(i) VOCAMix, a composition-aware augmentation that expands the variety of verb–object combinations, and
(ii) TORC, a temporal order regularization loss that promotes temporally grounded verb learning over static object cues.
Following prior work [ 16 ] , we use AIM [ 37 ] , a CLIP-based [ 28 ] parameter-efficient spatio-temporal encoder, as our backbone.

4.1 Composition-Aware Augmentation
To alleviate the sparsity of compositional training data, we propose Verb–Object Composition-Aware Augmentation (VOCAMix), which synthesizes plausible but unseen combinations while preserving the temporal structure of the primary video.
As shown in Figure 4 (b), VOCAMix replaces the motion region of a video with a static object region from another sample in the mini-batch.

4.2 Temporal Order Regularization Loss
To counter object-driven shortcuts in verb learning, we introduce the Temporal Order Regularization for Composition (TORC) loss.
TORC loss forces the model to rely on temporal structure: it penalizes alignment with temporally incorrect feature sequences and suppresses confident verb predictions when temporal ordering is corrupted.
This regularization steers the model away from static object cues and strengthens temporally grounded verb representations.

5.1 Experimental setup
Limitations of conventional ZS-CAR evaluation.
Existing ZS-CAR works [ 16 , 13 , 14 ] rely on the closed-world protocol, where inference is restricted to a small set of compositions that appear in the validation or test split.
This protocol hides a model’s incorrect tendency to over-predict seen compositions and obscures co-occurrence-driven behaviors.
A more serious methodological flaw is the use of test-set–tuned bias calibration.
Selecting the bias term with access to test labels systematically inflates unseen accuracy and prevents meaningful comparison across methods.
Our evaluation setup.
To expose genuine generalization, we adopt an open-world, unbiased protocol by default:
(i) inference spans the full space 𝕐 V × 𝕐 O \mathbb{Y}^{V}\times\mathbb{Y}^{O} , and
(ii) no test labels are used to tune biases.
We also report:
(a) open-world biased results using a realistic validation set -tuned bias, and
(b) closed-world H.M. and AUC for comparison with existing methods.
All results in Section 3 also follow the default open-world, unbiased protocol.
Datasets.
We evaluate on two ZS-CAR benchmarks: Sth-com [ 16 ] and our curated EK100-com.
Sth-com is derived from Something-Something V2 [ 12 ] and Something-Else [ 22 ] ,
containing 79K videos with 161 verbs and 248 objects.
Following prior work [ 39 , 31 ] , we also evaluate on the Temporal subset consisting of verbs requiring temporal reasoning.
We additionally introduce the EPIC-KITCHENS-100-composition (EK100-com) benchmark, constructed by repurposing EPIC-KITCHENS-100 [ 7 ] following the Sth-com protocol.
EK100-com includes 71K egocentric videos, 82 verbs, and 228 objects.
Full construction details are provided in the Section A .
Evaluation metrics.
We report top-1 composition, verb, and object accuracy on seen and unseen compositions, along with their harmonic mean (H.M.).
We also measure the compositional gap Δ CG \Delta_{\mathrm{CG}} ( 1 ) which indicates whether a model benefits from compositional reasoning beyond independent verb/object predictions.
(see Section 3 )
A higher Δ CG \Delta_{\mathrm{CG}} reflects stronger compositional synergy.
Baselines.
We primarily compare RCORE against C2C [ 16 ] , the current SOTA ZS-CAR method.
To isolate the effect of conditional learning, we also evaluate two independent baselines.
AIM [ 37 ] is the CLIP [ 28 ] -based spatio-temporal adapter model used as our backbone.
C2C w/o conditioning augments AIM with all architectural components of C2C except the conditional modeling itself.
We additionally include closed-world results of a recent ZS-CAR approach [ 14 ] .

5.2 Analysis
In this section, we validate that our RCORE framework effectively addresses the two key challenges in ZS-CAR—(i) reliance on co-occurrence statistics and (ii) object-driven shortcuts in verb learning—and achieves improved compositional representations compared to the baseline [ 16 ] .
Overcoming reliance on co-occurrence statistics.
In Figure 5 (a), we present the False Co-occurrence Prediction (FCP) curves of RCORE and the baseline [ 16 ] on Sth-com.
While the baseline’s FCP ratio increases substantially during training (11% → \rightarrow 17%), the FCP of RCORE decreases (9% → \rightarrow 8%), indicating that RCORE is markedly less dependent on co-occurrence statistics.
Addressing object-driven shortcuts.
In Figure 5 (b), we compare the cosine similarity between the original verb features 𝐟 V \mathbf{f}^{V} and the reversed verb features 𝐟 rev V \mathbf{f}^{V}_{\text{rev}} for RCORE and the baseline [ 16 ] over the course of training.
While the baseline [ 16 ] maintains a high cosine similarity ( 0.91 0.91 ) due to its reliance on object-driven shortcuts, RCORE drives this value to a strongly negative ( − 0.73 -0.73 ), successfully distinguishing opposite temporal semantics such as ’opening’ vs . ’closing’.
In Figure 6 , we further visualize this behavior through verb confusion matrices on the Sth-com [ 16 ] test set.
RCORE cleanly separates pairs of opposite verbs, while C2C [ 16 ] frequently confuses them, e.g . misclassifying ‘unfolding’ as ‘folding’.
These results collectively demonstrate that C2C fails to overcome the critical challenge of object-driven shortcuts in verb learning, whereas RCORE directly targets this failure mode and learns verb representations that generalize robustly to unseen compositions.
The learned verb representations are indeed effective.
We further assess the quality of the learned verb representations by evaluating temporal modeling ability on the Temporal subset of Sth-com [ 16 ] , as shown in Figure 5 (c).
To measure a model’s dependence on static cues, we compare its performance when using temporally shuffled verb features 𝐟 shuffled V \mathbf{f}^{V}_{\text{shuffled}} versus the original features 𝐟 V \mathbf{f}^{V} .
Across both seen and unseen compositions, RCORE exhibits a substantially larger performance gap between original and shuffled features. This demonstrates that its verb representations are effectively grounded in the temporal dynamics of the input.
Improved unseen generalization.
In Figure 5 (a), we present the learning curve of our RCORE and the baseline [ 16 ] on Sth-com.
Addressing the two key challenges in ZS-CAR, RCORE significantly improves unseen composition accuracy upon the baseline.
While the baseline significantly increases FCP ratio from 10.8% at 5 epochs to 16.8% at 25 epochs, we observe our RCORE reports FCP ratio values of 10.8% at 5 epochs and 8.7% at 25 epochs, demonstrating stable mitigation of the co-occurrence bias.
Notably, we also see a reduction in the seen-unseen accuracy gap.

5.4 Ablation Studies
Effects of RCORE components.
In Table 4 (a), we investigate the effect of each component in our RCORE framework.
When used individually, TORC loss is the most effective by providing explicit temporal modeling objectives.
Notably, it significantly improves verb recognition performances across both seen and unseen compositions (63.6% vs. 65.7% on seen compositions and 54.4% vs. 56.8% on unseen compositions).
Importantly, we can achieve the highest ZS-CAR performance by employing all three components together during training.
This synergistic improvement is achieved by effectively tackling dataset sparsity with VOCAMix, reinforcing temporal order modeling with TORC, and alleviating co-occurrence bias with Margin loss.
Effects of TORC components.
Table 4 (b) evaluates the roles of L cos L_{\cos} , which enforces discrimination of opposite temporal semantics, and L ent L_{\text{ent}} , which prevents reliance on static cues.
We show the each component of TORC can encourage performance improvement.
Each term individually improves performance, while using both together yields the largest gains in unseen verb accuracy.
Effects of VOCAMix.
In Table 4 (c), we validate the effectiveness of our proposed composition-aware VOCAMix by comparing it with widely adopted mixing augmentations.
We argue that conventional image-based augmentations are insufficient for composition verb-object learning.
Specifically, CutMix [ 38 ] allows for mixing backgrounds with corresponding labels and Mixup [ 41 ] blends verbs and objects concurrently, failing to preserve the temporal difference information that is essential for verb recognition.
As a result, these methods yield a lower H.M. score than the baseline.
In contrast, our VOCAMix, aiming to generate realistic unseen composition samples, shows modest performance gains over the baseline.
Furthermore, we observe that mixing a static frame into the estimated foreground region shows additional performance boost (+0.2 points in the H.M.) over applying it to the entire background (denoted as ‘VOCAMix w/o F.E.’).
Effects of Margin loss.
In Table 4 (d), we validate the effectiveness of our proposed Margin loss.
To mitigate the model’s reliance on dataset co-occurrence priors while maintaining baseline performance, we employ our method and validate its effectiveness by comparing it with the widely-used large-margin softmax loss.
The large-margin softmax (L-softmax) [ 19 ] loss is implemented by multiplying the angle θ \theta between the input feature vector and the target classifier by a margin m m ( e.g . , cos ⁡ ( m ​ θ ) \cos(m\theta) ), thereby forcing the model to learn stricter decision boundaries with narrower angular margins.
We apply this L-softmax loss into composition classification loss,
consistent with the implementation schedule of our Margin loss.
Compared to the L-softmax [ 19 ] approach, our proposed Margin loss successfully reduces FCP ratio while preserving performance.
This demonstrates the effectiveness of our strategy, which selectively targets frequent-but-incorrect logits not the entire logits.
6 Conclusions
We revisit zero-shot compositional action recognition and show that existing methods fail mainly due to object-driven shortcuts, stemming from compositional sparsity and the asymmetric difficulty of learning verbs versus objects.
We also find that the widely used closed-world, test-tuned evaluation protocol conceals this failure, overstating model generalization.
We introduce RCORE , a simple framework that targets these issues directly:
VOCAMix enlarges the effective compositional support, and TORC loss enforces temporal order sensitivity to reduce reliance on static object cues.
Across two benchmarks and under a realistic open-world, unbiased evaluation setting, RCORE consistently improves unseen composition recognition performances, indicating genuine compositional reasoning.
Our results highlight that both proper evaluation and shortcut-aware training are essential for progress in compositional video understanding.

Appendix A Details on EK100-com dataset
In this section, we provide details about our curated ZS-CAR benchmark, EPIC-KITCHENS-100-composition (EK100-com).
We construct EK100-com by repurposing EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (EK100) [ 7 ] following the same protocol of constructing Sth-com [ 16 ] .
In particular, we use the original training (67217 samples) and validation (9668 samples) split of EK100 [ 7 ] and split them as follows:
(1) we filter the data to include only compositions with more than five samples each.
(2) we ensure that all compositions present in the validation set also exist in the training set.
After initial filtering, the training set comprises 62,790 samples with 1,331 unique compositions and the validation set contains 8,657 samples, which consist of 833 seen compositions and 3 unseen compositions.
(3) we randomly select half of the compositions from both the training and validation sets and swap these subsets.
(4) Finally, we split the validation and test set with a ratio of 3 : 4 3:4 .
We provide the statistics of EK100-com in Table 5 and Figure 7 , and some seen/unseen composition examples of EK100-com in Figure 8 .
Beyond expanding the pool of publicly available ZS-CAR benchmarks, our repurposed EK100-com exhibits two key properties that make it a compelling ZS-CAR benchmark.
First, unlike Something-Something V2 [ 12 ] , where videos may involve multiple objects associated with a verb, videos in EK100 [ 7 ] depict actions consisting of a single verb and a single object.
Therefore, the training data of EK100-com provides explicit object supervision for the models.
Second, since EK100 [ 7 ] has long-tailed distribution, the label coverage ratio of EK100-com is 7.5%, which is much lower than that of Sth-com [ 16 ] (12.8%).
This makes EK100-com a challenging benchmark, suitable for evaluating whether a model can overcome the risk of shortcut learning induced by data sparsity.

B.1 Implementation details on our diagnosis
In this section, we provide comprehensive details of experimental setup and implementation details of our diagnosis for Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) in Section 3 in the main paper.
All notations used in this supplementary document are consistent with those defined in the main paper.
As mentioned in the main paper, we adopt the state-of-the-arts model, C2C [ 16 ] which uses a conditional learning approach, as the existing ZS-CAR baseline for diagnosis.
Details about our diagnosis in Figure 2 (a).
In Figure 2 (a) in the main paper, we empirically demonstrate the asymmetric learning difficulty between verbs and objects.
We train a randomly initialized ViT [ 10 ] with joint spatio-temporal attention on our selected subset of the Sth-com [ 16 ] dataset.
We aim to select a subset that maximizes the number of samples while maintaining a sufficient number of distinct labels.
As a result, the selected subset is composed of 10 verb classes: ‘Moving sth and sth away from each other’, ‘Moving sth and sth closer to each other’, ‘Moving sth away from sth’, ‘Moving sth closer to sth’, ‘Moving sth down’, ‘Moving sth up’, ‘Pushing sth from left to right’, ‘Pushing sth from right to left’, ‘Pushing sth so that it falls off the table’, and ‘Pushing sth so that it slightly moves’; and 10 object classes: ‘Ball’, ‘Battery’, ‘Book’, ‘Bottle’, ‘Coin’, ‘Glass’, ‘Knife’, ‘Paper’, ‘Remote’, and ‘Spoon’.
We construct the training set consisting of 2,555 samples from the original Sth-Com [ 16 ] training and validation samples, while the validation set comprises 260 samples from the original Sth-Com [ 16 ] test set.
For training, we employ a multi-task learning approach using separate linear classifiers for verbs and objects, taking the ViT’s CLS token as input.
In the main paper, we show that objects are easier to learn than verbs by monitoring the learning curves of a randomly initialized ViT.
Furthermore, we substantiate in Section C demonstrating that this asymmetric learning difficulty leads the model to exploit object-driven shortcuts in compositional video understanding.

The training set consists of the four diagonal pairs (refer to Figure 2 (b)) with 40 samples per pair.
The test set comprises two distinct splits: seen compositions (25 samples per pair) and unseen compositions (30 samples per pair).
We use 8 frames for input videos.

B.2 Implementation details on RCORE
Experimental Setup.
We implement our method using PyTorch and conduct all experiments on 8 NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs.
For video preprocessing, we uniformly sample frames from each video to generate clips of size 3 × 16 × 224 × 224 3\times 16\times 224\times 224 (channels × \times frames × \times height × \times width).
Model Architecture.
We utilize CLIP-B/16 [ 28 ] as our visual/text backbone.
Following prior work [ 16 ] , we adopt AIM [ 37 ] , a parameter-efficient spatio-temporal adapter for CLIP [ 28 ] , as the video encoder.
We also construct the verb encoder with two temporal convolution layers with ReLU activations, while the object encoder employs temporal average pooling followed by a two-layer MLP with ReLU activations.
We use CoOp-style [ 43 ] learnable text prompts for all models.
Training Strategy.
We train all models, including baselines and RCORE , for 30 epochs with a total batch size of 128.
The base learning rate is set to 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} for Sth-com [ 16 ] and 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} for EK100-com, initialized with a 3-epoch warmup.
Following prior work [ 16 ] , we adopt closed-world training setting.
We empirically find that setting the softmax temperature to 0.07, same as the implementation of CLIP [ 28 ] , results in better ZS-CAR performance than the value of 0.01, used in prior work [ 16 ] .
Therefore, we adopt this temperature value for both C2C [ 16 ] and RCORE , except for the case of AIM [ 37 ] with independent modeling.
For VOCAMix, we employ the unsupervised foreground estimation algorithm FAME [ 9 ] to identify high-motion regions.
FAME [ 9 ] isolates the moving foreground from background regions based on frame differences and color statistics.
To generate the mixed samples, we first sample the mixing coefficient from a Beta ​ ( 2.0 , 2.0 ) \text{Beta}(2.0,2.0) distribution, following prior work [ 38 , 41 ] .
We then scale it by 0.2 for Sth-com [ 16 ] and 0.5 for EK100-com to obtain the final blending coefficient λ \lambda .

Loss configuration.
For the total loss, we set the weights for the verb and object components to α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 and for the composition loss to β = 1.0 \beta=1.0 , following prior work [ 16 ] .
As demonstrated in Table 9 (g) and (h), we empirically find it beneficial to linearly warm up the weights for the auxiliary losses: γ \gamma is increased from 0.0 to 1.0 over 5 epoch to 10 epoch, and δ \delta from 0.0 to 0.8 over epochs 15 epoch to 20 epoch.
Inference.
During inference, we adopt a single-view, single-crop protocol.
For bias calibration, we select the bias term that maximizes the harmonic mean of the accuracies for seen and unseen compositions.

Appendix C Additional Evidence of Object-Driven Shortcuts
In this section, we provide further evidence demonstrating that existing ZS-CAR learning approaches are susceptible to object-driven shortcut learning.
Failure case analysis of the existing ZS-CAR model.
In Table 7 and Table 8 , we investigate top-10 failure cases of the model trained with the existing ZS-CAR learning approach [ 16 ] .
The top-10 failure cases shown in the Table 7 constitute 9.5% of the misclassifications on unseen compositions for Sth-com [ 16 ] , compared to 49% for EK100-com as shown in Table 8 .
For the analysis of Sth-com [ 16 ] , we exclude ambiguous cases arising from annotation issues to obtain meaningful results.
A prime example is the top-1 failure case, (‘Covering [something] with [something]’, ‘Paper’), where 66% of the errors are misclassified as ‘Pencil’.
Upon visual inspection, we confirm that nearly all these videos actually depict the action of covering a pencil with paper.
In Table 7 and Table 8 , we observe a common tendency across both datasets: the model frequently misclassifies verbs as their temporally reversed or opposing counterparts.
Specifically, we demonstrate that these mispredictions stem from the model’s reliance on co-occurrence statistics.
For instance, the model misclassifies unseen ‘(Closing, Drawer)’ samples as ‘(Opening, Drawer)’, which accounts for 36% of the errors.
Notably, ‘Opening’ is the verb most frequently paired with ‘Drawer’ in the training set.
These findings suggest that the model has failed to learn robust verb representations that generalize to unseen compositions, largely due to object-driven shortcut learning.

Appendix D Additional Results
D.1 Comprehensive ablation results
In Table 9 , we provide the comprehensive ablation study results to examine each design choice of RCORE , using the Sth-com [ 16 ] dataset.
Effects of TORC loss with different temporal aggregation methods.
In Table 9 (d), we demonstrate that the weak temporal order modeling caused by object-driven shortcut learning cannot be resolved merely by employing more sophisticated temporal aggregation methods.
We compare the baseline’s temporal average pooling with attention pooling (Attn. pool). In attention pooling, a linear layer computes frame-wise attention weights from the input verb feature sequences, aggregating them via a weighted sum to obtain the final verb feature for classification.
While attention pooling yields a slight improvement in verb accuracy, it fails to reduce the compositional gap ( Δ C ​ G \Delta_{CG} ) on unseen compositions.
In contrast, our TORC loss achieves significant improvements in H.M. with both aggregation methods.
Notably, the combination of temporal average pooling and TORC loss enables the model to overcome the negative compositional gap.
Effects of top- K K selection for Margin loss.
In Table 9 (e), we investigate the impact of the hyperparameter K K , which determines the number of top-ranked logits to which the Margin loss is applied.
We find that applying the margin selectively to the frequent-but-incorrect logits within the top-10 ( K = 10 K=10 ) reports the highest H.M., outperforming the approach of applying it to all seen composition logits ( K = 3451 K=3451 ) (36.4% vs. 35.5%).
This suggests that penalizing only the most confusing candidates—specifically those that frequently co-occur with the input components—effectively mitigates co-occurrence bias without compromising the model’s overall performance.
For instance, given an input like ‘(Pretending to tear, Paper)’, our intention is to penalize plausible but incorrect distractors such as ‘(Tearing, Paper)’ or ‘(Folding, Paper)’, while avoiding penalties on irrelevant classes like ‘(Throwing, Paper)’ that are already ranked low.

We present extended results corresponding to the experiment shown in Figure 5 (c) of the main paper, including all versions of the Temporal/Static split.
Inspired by prior work [ 31 , 39 ] , we rigorously evaluate the temporal modeling capabilities of both the baseline (C2C [ 16 ] ) and our RCORE by partitioning the Sth-com [ 16 ] dataset into Temporal and Static splits.
Sevilla et al. [ 31 ] originally defined these splits based on cognitive science experiments on Something-Something V2 [ 12 ] verb classes: a Temporal split (18 verbs) where temporal information matters, and a Static split (18 verbs) where such information is redundant.
However, noting that this Temporal split includes verbs requiring complex temporal reasoning such as ‘Folding’, we reconfigure the splits based on verb semantics.
Specifically, we categorized verbs based on this criterion: those requiring temporal information for discrimination are assigned to the Temporal split (62 verbs), while verbs distinguishable by momentary keyframes are assigned to the Static split (80 verbs).
